column3: A communal confession of sins and request for forgiveness parallels the focus's acknowledged wrongdoing, but lacks its death-and-exit setting.
It places idolaters in the Fire without helpers, providing a consequence horizon for the focus's request to escape.
The claim that there is no obligation toward others does not clarify repeated death, confession, or a possible exit.
Believers ask forgiveness for sins and a righteous death, offering a faithful counterpart to the focus's belated confession.
The accusation against the messenger begins the surah's opposition context but does not add to the focus's plea.
It directly voices disbelief that one who has died can be brought forth alive, framing the reversal affirmed in the focus.
Its plea for forgiveness and protection from the Fire closely parallels the focus's confession, though without an exit question.
Their return to Hell directly frames the destination from which the speakers in the focus seek a way out.
It explicitly joins life from death, revival after death, and eventual human emergence, directly clarifying the focus's repeated death-life-exit sequence.
The inhabitants of the blaze acknowledge their sin, an especially close parallel to the focus's confession within punishment.
Entrusting one's affair to God later in the same surah offers a response to warning, but not the focus's post-judgment plea.
Its failed promise of accompanying an expelled group concerns social abandonment, not an exit from accounted consequences.
The proposed payment called kharj is a different use of the term and does not clarify the focus's requested release.
Reviving dead land through descending provision offers a broad sign of life after death, now redundant after 30:19.
Its contrasts between expulsion and striving are worldly and do not explain the focus's eschatological exit.
Inheritance shares and the number two do not illuminate the paired deaths and lives of the focus.
Divine signs and provision establish a nearby surah theme of remembrance but do not clarify the confession or exit.
The refusal to make an exception is unrelated to the focus's two deaths and two lives.
Musa's prayer names a path from which Pharaoh's people stray, but it does not illuminate the focus's final request for a path out.
Return to God and provision after idolatry are too general to add to the focus's punishment-and-exit scene.
The repeated seven and the great Quran do not clarify the focus's repeated deaths and lives.
When the outcome arrives, people admit the messengers brought truth and ask to be returned to act differently, closely paralleling the focus's belated plea for another way.
The command for sincere devotion supplies an earlier-surah alternative to the speakers' delayed recognition, but only indirectly.
Blocking God's path supplies a general cause of misguidance, not a focused link to the requested exit.
Those facing punishment ask whether others can avert it, and the answer declares no escape, directly delimiting the focus's hope for a way out.
Provision for creatures does not clarify death, confession, or the eschatological exit.
It calls a reminder a route to the Lord, a broad positive counterpart to the focus's question about whether any route remains.
Inheritance rules and the numerical phrase do not clarify the focus.
The contrast of believer and evildoer in the same surah gives a moral backdrop but adds little to the plea.
A lasting roadway by ruined towns is unrelated to the focus's path of release.
The people of the Garden ask the people of the Fire whether the promise proved true, supplying a direct scene of post-judgment recognition.
Its contrast between fleeting worldly life and the living hereafter supports the focus's life-after-death horizon, though indirectly.
Waiting for someone to come out is a social instruction, not a relation to the focus's requested exit.
Trust in the Living who does not die contrasts divine permanence with human death, but does not explain repeated revival.
Creation, form, and provision in the same surah do not add to confession or an exit from punishment.
Being brought forth for humankind concerns communal responsibility, not the focus's resurrection and plea.
The oppressed explicitly ask their Lord to bring them out of an unjust town, a worldly but clear counterpart to the focus's appeal for exit.
Sins leading to affliction provide a broad accountability link, but not the focus's death-life or release question.
It explicitly combines living on earth, dying there, and being brought forth from it, closely clarifying the focus's death-life-exit pattern.
Future recognition of divine signs gives a general counterpart to the focus's acknowledgment, without its consequence or plea.
Warning of the Day of Meeting in the same surah supplies proximate judgment context but not the focus's particular request.
Gathering to Hell and being far astray describes an adverse destination, but does not add to the focus beyond that context.
The call to submit after revelation is an earlier alternative to the focus's late acknowledgment, but only generally.
Its tree emerging from Hell is a different use of emergence and does not clarify a human exit from punishment.
Entry conditioned on tyrants leaving is a worldly military decision, not the focus's eschatological release.
Hearing revelation leads to faith and a prayer to be counted among witnesses, a faithful contrast to the focus's delayed confession.
The angels ask forgiveness and protection from Hell for those who repent and follow God's path, directly supplying the viable counterpart to the focus's plea.
God gives life and causes death, confirming divine command over both states, though it adds no exit dimension.
Expulsion from homes and reluctance to fight do not clarify the focus's death-and-resurrection plea.
The rebuke of worshipping Baal does not add a focused relation to the confession or exit question.
Persisting blindness and greater loss of the path in the hereafter give a broad warning about the state from which the focus seeks release.
The prohibition on two gods does not clarify the focus's paired deaths and lives.
It declares return to God and identifies the excessive as companions of the Fire, directly situating the focus's speakers and their appeal.
The objection to resurrection from death, dust, and bones closely frames the repeated revival asserted by the focus, though it repeats 19:66.
Following the path of those who turn to God before the final return offers a broad alternative to the focus's belated request.
The divine word that disbelievers are companions of the Fire gives immediate surah context for the focus's constrained exit question.
Calling an inheritance-marriage practice an evil path does not clarify the focus's path out of punishment.
The slain being alive with their Lord qualifies ordinary death, but does not develop the focus's repeated death-and-life sequence.
Reviving the earth after its death is a sign of restoration, but it is a redundant indirect parallel after 30:19 and 45:5.
The hand emerging white is a miraculous sign, not a relation to resurrection or post-judgment exit.
The same divine agent causes death and then gives life, directly clarifying the central reversal named in the focus.
Disbelievers disputing divine signs offers nearby opposition context but not the focus's confession or request.
The command to leave under a curse is an expulsion, but it contrasts with rather than explains the focus's hoped-for exit.
Migration undertaken for God and interrupted by death is a voluntary worldly departure, only distantly related to the focus's release.
The contrast between killing and preserving life concerns human conduct, not the divine death-and-revival sequence.
Competing paths in battle do not clarify an exit from the Fire.
Witness procedures at the time of death do not add to the focus's resurrection or confession.
God forgives sin, accepts repentance, and is severe in punishment; this is immediate context for both the focus's confession and its uncertain hope of release.
The comparison of religious service and striving does not clarify the focus's request for a way out.
The oath opening does not add to death, life, confession, or exit.
Creation of male and female pairs does not clarify the focus's two deaths and two lives.
It disputes that the dead reduced to dust and bones can be brought out, a close but now redundant resurrection objection.
A candid admission of sin and request for forgiveness parallels the focus's confession, without its final-judgment setting.
The same surah contrasts proportionate recompense for evil with entry to the Garden for believers, clarifying the moral stakes behind the plea.
It tersely states that God causes death and gives life, but adds little after fuller earlier parallels.
Adam and his spouse confess wrongdoing and seek forgiveness and mercy, an important pre-punishment counterpart to the focus's belated confession.
The bad return of transgressors gives a general punishment destination but does not clarify the requested exit.
The instruction not to die except in submission offers a broad contrast to dying in the condition implied by the focus.
A prayer for steadfastness in battle does not add to the focus's confession or exit.
Provision through livestock in the same surah does not clarify the focus's plea.
The command to fight in God's path does not illuminate repeated death and revival.
Two messengers reinforced by a third does not clarify the focus's paired deaths and lives.
It explicitly orders creation, provision, death, and life under God, directly supporting the death-life premise though redundant at this rank.
It states the certainty of later death but adds no revival, confession, or exit beyond the established sequence.
Believers pray for forgiveness and mercy, supplying another faithful counterpart to the focus's acknowledged sin.
Earlier communities' rejection and punishment offer nearby judgment context but do not clarify the focus's words.
The shown path and human gratitude or ingratitude provide a broad antecedent to the accountability scene in the focus.
Those who followed leaders acknowledge being led astray from the path, a post-consequence confession that sharpens the focus's admission of guilt.
Dying in disbelief and remaining under a comprehensive curse gives a grave finality contrast to the focus's request for another exit.
A community's challenge for promised punishment does not clarify the focus's two deaths, two lives, or confession.
The wish to delay an appointed term reflects fear of death, but does not develop the focus's resurrection and release.
A demonstrated ability to revive the dead supports the focus's death-life premise, but is redundant after the direct statements.
Human developmental stages and dead land revived by rain provide an extended sign for resurrection, though later and indirect.
Those in the Fire repeatedly seek to leave but are returned to it, directly answering the focus's question about whether any exit remains.
The demand for the promised decision is eschatological challenge, but it does not clarify confession, revival, or exit.
At a single call people come forth from the earth, directly explaining how post-death emergence occurs and reinforcing the focus's hope of reversal.
The judgment inquiry distinguishes self-led from externally induced misguidance, only broadly related to acknowledged wrongdoing.
Faith and striving in God's path do not clarify the focus's post-punishment appeal for a path out.
Guidance to a straight path provides a general positive contrast to the focus's question whether any path remains.
The Fire's inhabitants neither die nor receive reduced punishment, directly clarifying the severe finality that makes the focus's request for exit urgent.
The preceding call to the disbelievers explains the judgment setting in which the speakers of the focus recognize their own rejection.
The following verse gives the reason their requested exit is denied: they rejected God when called to Him alone.
Those in the Fire ask its keepers to seek even one day's reduction of punishment, a direct parallel to the focus's plea for release.
The keepers answer that their messengers brought proofs and that the disbelievers' supplication goes astray, directly constraining the focus's hope.
God gives life, causes death, and brings a matter into being by command, directly grounding the focus's two deaths and two lives.
The people in the Fire ask their Lord to bring them out and promise changed conduct, the closest direct parallel to the focus's exit request.
The answer commanding them to remain in the Fire directly supplies the negative outcome left open by the focus's question.
At death a person asks to be sent back in order to act rightly, closely paralleling a belated request for another passage.
The refusal of return and the barrier until resurrection directly limits the possibility of a post-death reversal.
Criminals confess, say they have seen and heard, and ask to be sent back for righteous action, closely matching the focus's remorse and request.
The trumpet causes death and then a later blast raises all to look on, directly clarifying the repeated death-life sequence.
It explicitly orders being lifeless, receiving life, dying, receiving life again, and returning to God, a foundational parallel to the focus's paired sequence.
Humanity is brought from earth, returned to it, and brought forth once more, directly joining death, burial, and emergence.
The trumpet blast brings people forth from graves toward their Lord, directly depicting the emergence implied by the focus.
The One who originates creation and repeats it provides a concise basis for life being restored after its first course ends.
God gives life, then death, then life again, directly paralleling the focus's stated sequence.
God gives life, causes death, and gathers all for the Day without doubt, directly framing the focus's post-judgment speech.
The day people hear the blast in truth is explicitly called the day of coming forth, directly clarifying the requested emergence.
The revival of dead land is explicitly followed by the assurance that people will likewise be brought out.
Those in graves are raised by God and returned to Him, directly joining resurrection and final return.
God gives life and death, and to Him people return, a compact direct parallel to the focus's premise.
Divine dominion includes giving life and causing death, directly supporting the focus's attribution of both states to the Lord.
Death and life are both created as a test, providing a direct theological frame for their sequence in the focus.
The challenge over whether bones can be gathered directly addresses the bodily restoration presupposed by the focus.
The One who creates human life is declared able to give life to the dead, directly supporting the focus's reversal of death.
The deniers ask whether they will be restored after the first death, closely matching the resurrection question behind the focus.
Their objection specifically invokes decayed bones, sharpening the material-resurrection issue in the focus.
God tells a multitude fleeing death to die and then gives them life, an exceptional but close death-to-life reversal.
A man is caused to die for a long period and then raised, supplying a concrete sign of restoration after death.
God brings the living from the dead and the dead from the living, a close cosmic parallel to the focus's paired states.
A person made alive after being dead and given light supplies a secondary life-from-death counterpart.
The question about bringing living from dead and dead from living supplies a concise counterpart to the focus's sequence.
The objection to being raised after becoming bones and fragments frames the resurrection the focus assumes has occurred.
The repeated denial of resurrection from bones and dust supplies a close contrast to the focus's acknowledgment of revival.
The three marked moments of birth, death, and being raised alive give a compact life-death-resurrection pattern.
The same birth, death, and rising-alive pattern is voiced in the first person, closely echoing the focus's self-description.
It states that the Hour is coming and that those in graves will be raised, directly setting the eschatological horizon.
After death, people are raised on the Day of Resurrection, completing the immediate sequence begun in 23:15.
The inhabitants of the Fire acknowledge that the Lord's signs were recited to them and that they denied, preceding their plea to be brought out.
The objection to resurrection after becoming dust, together with forefathers, provides a close denial contrast.
The angel of death takes people and they are then returned to their Lord, directly situating death within return rather than cessation.
God gives life to the dead and records what people sent ahead, linking revival with the accountability acknowledged in the focus.
The question of who can revive decayed bones is a direct challenge to the resurrection affirmed by the focus.
The answer that the first creator revives bones directly answers that challenge and supports the focus's life-after-death claim.
God takes souls at death and returns some during sleep, clarifying divine control over death and return to life.
The command not to despair of divine mercy supplies a living-world contrast to the focus's late confession under judgment.
The Day when all come forth and nothing is hidden from God directly supplies the setting of full exposure behind the focus's admission.
Pharaoh's people are exposed to the Fire and then enter its severer punishment at the Hour, a nearby surah model of irreversible consequence.
The people of the Fire dispute there, reinforcing that the focus's speech belongs to a real post-judgment exchange.
The arrogant in the Fire declare that all are in it and that God has judged among His servants, directly limiting an escape route.
The warning that the proud will enter Hell humbled contrasts delayed acknowledgment with the timely calling on God.
Reviving dead earth is given as a sign that the One who does so gives life to the dead.
The claim that return after death and dust is far off gives a direct denial contrast to the focus's experienced return.
Dead land revived by rain is explicitly made a sign of coming forth from graves.
The command to listen for the near call prepares the paired description of the day of emergence.
The assertion that the dead will be raised is emphatically affirmed, directly supporting the focus's resurrection premise.
The One who creates the human being is declared fully able to return him, a concise restoration parallel.
No human is granted immortality, establishing mortality but not the focus's subsequent revival or plea.
Every soul tastes death and is tested, providing a broad mortality-and-accountability setting.
Wind and rain revive dead land, an indirect sign of resurrection already represented by stronger candidates.
The people of the Garden do not taste death beyond the first, offering a contrasting eschatological finality.
The objection to being raised after death, dust, and bones repeats a resurrection-denial pattern already represented more directly.
The reminder that God created humanity provides only a broad basis for the power to recreate.
Earth holding the living and the dead gives a spatial counterpart to burial and later emergence, but only indirectly.
Its pairing of the living and dead continues that broad earth-as-container image without stating revival.
